newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Stockpile treads gingerly in cobalt market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Stockpile treads gingerly in cobalt market.

text.p: Armed with as much metal as a major producer, the U.S. government stockpile is treading gingerly through the intimate world of cobalt.

The Defense Authorisation Bill - sent to President Clinton Tuesday for approval - states that 26 million pounds (11,794 tonnes) of cobalt is surplus to requirements and should be sold off over ten years to raise cash for the Treasury.
Some 14 million pounds of additional metal was set aside for defense purposes and is not up for grabs.

In the fiscal year starting October 1, the Defense Logisitics Agency which adminsters the government's commodities stash, will have a maximum six million pounds of cobalt to sell, stockpile administrator Richard Connelly stressed in a presentation at the Gorham/Intertech cobalt conference Wednesday.
The DLA supplies about a third of U.S. cobalt demand each year, and the fate of the extra metal for sale arouses concern among some in the cobalt industry.

With analysts and others at the conference predicting a sharp rise in supply by the turn of the decade, some delagates suggested privately that the stockpile may feel it necessary to sell more sooner rather than later to maximize earnings.
"I did not hear much this morning that suggested to me that it will maximise taxpayers revenue by being conservative," Connelly said.

The stockpile is subject to regulations that it does not unduly disrupt the market, and Connelly sought industry opinions by October 30 as to whether all or part of this year's allocation could be sold under a sealed or negotiated bid, and what grades should be offered.
An advisory committee suggested the negotiated bid process was consistent with industry practices, though some believed it has led to a loss of some transparency in the market.
"Some people say they won't play under sealed bid because it's too public, but competition is a good thing for us," Connelly said.
Sales should also not be scheduled during industry summer shutdowns and holidays, the advisory committee also suggested.
"We are going to try them (the advisory committee suggestions) for a year and see what we and you think and what the industry thinks how they are working," Connelly told delegates.
"How much we are going to sell depends on what response we get from the market," Connelly added.
